papers.title: Text-to-music Generation via Structured Captions AND Interpretable Evaluation
papers.abstract: Text descriptions of music are central to the performance of text-to-music generation (TTM) methods, but creation of paired text information for music generation is relatively under explored. Here, we propose training latent diffusion/flow-based music generation models conditioned on structured captions (SCAPs) and compare with typical free-form captions via a set of controlled ablations. We compare free-form vs. structured captions, partial vs. full information coverage, and global vs. temporal text information during training, by fine-tuning different configurations of a pretrained flow-based diffusion transformer (DiT) and using a multi-stage inference-time prompt rewriter. Further, we introduce a new text-alignment evaluation protocol inspired by Davidsonian Scene Graphs (DSGs) for a fine-grained, interpretable measure of faithfulness of TTM methods. With multiple metrics, we show 1) that fine-tuning our DiT on SCAPs significantly improves text-alignment on music generation outputs while also improving quality, and 2) our proposed Music DSG metric better correlates with human preference than CLAP.
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: text-to-music, music generation

papers.title: Zero-Shot Voice Cloning for Synthetic Data Augmentation in Children's ASR
papers.abstract: Children's automatic speech recognition (ASR) lags behind adult ASR due to theacoustic mismatch between adult-trained acoustic models and children's speech, as well as the scarcity of labelled children's speech corpora. We investigate whether zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis with voice cloning, requiring only a short reference clip per speaker, can serve as a practical substitute for real children's speech when fine-tuning large pre-trained ASR models. Using the OmniVoice multilingual TTS system we synthesise up to 16,000 child-like utterances from two English corpora (ENNI, clinical narrative samples, ages 7-12, and MyST, conversational science-tutor speech, grades 3-5) and fine-tune Whisper-small under different experimental conditions covering real data, synthetic data, cross-corpus data, and all-data combination. A systematic sensitivity analysis over speaker count, text-pool size, and utterances per speaker reveals that synthetic data alone reduces word error rate (WER) from a 19.8 % zero-shot baseline to 16.4 % on ENNI, recovering approximately 30 % of the gap to real-data fine-tuning (8.8 %). Combining synthetic with real data is essentially indistinguishable from real-data-only fine-tuning (9.2 % vs. 8.8 %). Speaker count plateaus at ~40 speakers for cross-domain transfer, while multi-speaker acoustic diversity per transcript, rather than raw text coverage, emerges as the primary determinant of cross-domain generalisation; out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rate proves to be a poor proxy for WER given Whisper's pre-trained language modelling capacity.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech, automatic speech recognition, voice cloning

papers.title: Learning Timeline-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) increasingly preserves what is said and how it sounds, but not necessarily when speech and silence occur. For dubbing and other temporally grounded applications, matching total duration is not enough: speech and pauses must also occur at corresponding moments. We formulate timeline-preserving S2ST, which aims to preserve the source endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline. We present TransDubber, an end-to-end autoregressive system that learns this temporal structure directly from aligned target waveforms, without inference-time frame-level timing control or post-hoc temporal correction. To provide this supervision, we construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning to balance translation quality and temporal alignment. On a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber increases the proportion of translations within 2% of the source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS, while maintaining competitive translation quality. Our analysis shows that aligned supervision establishes timeline following, while reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partially offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our data and training framework for timeline-preserving S2ST. Audio samples, code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://zhishengzheng.com/transdubber/.

papers.title: ReplayFactor: Replay-Aware Dual-Attribute Learning for Practical Speech Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Advances in synthesis techniques have made deepfake speech increasingly realistic, amplifying voice security threats, including unauthorized voice cloning and impersonation. Although existing deepfake detectors perform well on digitally generated speech, their performance often degrades on physically replayed deepfakes, which constitute a low-cost and practical threat to real-world systems. Existing research focuses primarily on dataset construction and evaluation, while available dataset diversity and replay-aware detector design remain limited. We propose ReplayFactor, a dual-attribute framework that enhances replay evidence by fusing self-supervised learning (SSL) representations with an acoustic prior, while leveraging multi-task learning and supervised contrastive learning to promote robust, generalizable representations. We also construct ReplayFake-CN, a large-scale, multi-device Chinese dataset comprising approximately 185k replayed synthetic utterances to complement public benchmarks. Our framework improves macro-F1 from 60.99% to 76.44% and reduces EER from 11.86% to 3.05% on the EchoFake open set over the baseline, demonstrating strong potential for practical replayed deepfake detection.

papers.title: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Generative spoken language models (SLMs) offer a route to learning linguistic structure purely from speech, yet they lag far behind text-based models in both capability and data scaling efficiency. We identify two bottlenecks underlying this gap: the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and the reliance on a single stream of discrete units to represent speech. Multiple codebooks are widely used to encode acoustic features but rarely to represent speech semantics. We present GSLM2, which learns and models complementary properties of speech at multiple levels of abstraction. Its encoder, SpidR 2.0, uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce high-quality discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM then jointly models these units using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors, and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies. Across training data sizes and model scales, up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence while scaling more efficiently with data. As a result, it substantially narrows the gap between spoken and text-based LMs; across read and conversational speech domains, we shrink the gap by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC, while also outperforming competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks. We open-source the training code and model checkpoints at https://github.com/facebookresearch/gslm2.
papers.venue: Equal contribution by Yosuke Higuchi and Tom Fizycki. Core contribution by Mahi Luthra, Charles-Éric Saint-James and Azeez Syed

papers.title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.

papers.title: Spatial Transfusion: From Structured Spatial Scene Understanding to Generation and Editing
papers.abstract: Spatial audio conveys not only what sounds are present, but where they originate and how they interact with the environment. Recent audio-language models increasingly understand and reason about such scenes, yet spatial audio understanding, generation, and editing remain largely separate. We present Spatial Transfusion, a unified first-order ambisonics (FOA) framework that extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model to generation and editing through flow matching over VAE latents. We formulate editing as a structured scene transformation over a taxonomy of atomic edits. Keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, we introduce modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum that progressively adds generation, editing, and natural-language interaction. Experiments show that Spatial Transfusion largely preserves spatial understanding while outperforming full fine-tuning in generation and editing. The resulting model supports controllable FOA generation and editing through both structured and natural-language interfaces. Audio samples are available at https://microsoft.github.io/spatial-transfusion/

papers.title: How Close to the Theme? Similarity-Label Conditioning for Game Music Generation
papers.abstract: Composers develop music from an original idea, controlling how similar each new section is to it, from near repetition to new material. Game music needs this often, as its material repeats over long play. Music models, however, rarely learn to control similarity from real pieces. We further train a pretrained MIDI model on section pairs from Super Mario pieces. A label states each pair's similarity, and a context vector summarises the given section, or context. For 157 test contexts, the model generates six outputs per label. Twelve measures score the outputs; one main measure each covers melody, pitch content, rhythm and note length. On average, outputs requested as similar are more similar to their context than those requested as dissimilar, and not to other pieces. All twelve measures favour them; each main measure stays significant after correction for multiple tests. On melody, the gap comes mainly from more frequent restatement of the context's melody. Against an otherwise identical model without a label, only the request for high similarity makes outputs more similar. In a listening test, ratings followed melodic overlap with the context most closely of all measures.
papers.venue: 39 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables, including supplementary material. Submitted to Computer Music Journal

papers.title: MEX: The Musical Expectation Benchmark Suite
papers.abstract: We propose the Musical Expectation (MEX) benchmark suite for perceptually validating computational models of musical expectation, i.e., models that estimate music information dynamics (MID) measures of perceived musical expectations, such as surprisal or uncertainty from symbolic music or musical audio. MEX collects and extends tasks for evaluating such models previously proposed in music information retrieval and cognitive sciences using standard datasets, and evaluates whether: (1) proposed MID measures decrease with repetition due to in-context learning of the computational model, (2) peaks in such measures align with boundaries of music segments, (3) pitch surprisal and uncertainty estimated from audio are consistent with those modeled in event-based symbolic music, (4) proposed MID measures can predict electrophysiological responses to music. We stress that this benchmark suite does not provide an exhaustive computational characterization of music expectation. Rather, we envision this as an active, interdisciplinary initiative, with benchmarks evolving as our understanding of the underlying perceptual processes deepens. We provide open-access code https://github.com/musicperceptmodeling/mex to estimate surprisal and uncertainty from audio using baseline models, run the tasks on standard datasets, and include utilities for running the tasks with users' own data.
papers.venue: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 26th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, 2026

papers.title: Rel2Traj: Inter-Source Relation-Aware Trajectory Generation for Text-To-Spatial-Audio
papers.abstract: "A car drives from front left to front right while a dog follows it." Such a description specifies no particular trajectory, yet imposes a constraint on the joint motion of both sources that must hold at every frame. Existing text-to-spatial-audio methods can position and move each sound source according to its description, but none of them ensures or verifies that such inter-source relations hold. We therefore propose Rel2Traj, which parses the description into sources, relations, and anchors, jointly generates the trajectories of all sources using a relation-conditioned diffusion model, and finally renders sounds from a pretrained text-to-audio model along these trajectories to produce binaural audio. For training and evaluation, we construct a synthetic dataset from a controlled language of source motions and inter-source relations. A single frame-wise relational geometry defines both our evaluation metric, the Relation Satisfaction Rate (RSR), and an auxiliary training loss. On motion-relation combinations held out from training, Rel2Traj maintains all relation types, whereas every baseline fails on at least one. A listening test further confirms that listeners recognize the described relations. To our knowledge, this is the first text-to-spatial-audio work to model relations among moving sources as explicit geometric constraints.
papers.venue: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: text-to-audio

papers.title: Multilingual TASU: Extending Text-Only Alignment to Multilingual Speech Recognition via Simulated CTC Posteriors
papers.abstract: Speech Large Language Models (Speech LLMs) achieve strong multilingual ASR when large-scale paired speech-text data is available, yet such resources remain scarce and highly imbalanced across languages. Text-Only Alignment for Speech Understanding (TASU) alleviates this bottleneck by training cross-modal alignment from simulated CTC posteriors without paired audio, but prior work has been limited to English, leaving open whether text-driven alignment can scale to the multilingual setting where data sparsity and cross-lingual phonetic interference amplify the difficulty of learning a shared alignment interface. In this work, we investigate TASU-style posterior alignment as a means of mitigating paired-data scarcity in multilingual ASR. We adopt the native 50,002-way posterior space of a frozen OWSM-CTC frontend as a shared multilingual interface to Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and systematically compare three supervision sources on eight Multilingual LibriSpeech languages: real audio-derived posteriors, heuristic CTC Posterior Simulation (CPS), and posteriors generated by a learned multilingual simulator. With real posteriors, LoRA adaptation reduces pooled WER from 10.08% (standalone OWSM-CTC) to 8.21%, improving all eight languages. For text-only alignment, the learned simulator substantially outperforms heuristic CPS and attains 10.51% WER with LoRA. Notably, a CPS-initialized model reaches 9.19% WER after only one real-posterior adaptation epoch using merely one-ninth of the complete MLS paired-speech training set, demonstrating that text-first initialization can drastically reduce the amount of paired audio required for competitive multilingual ASR. These findings establish TASU as a viable multilingual alignment framework and highlight text-only simulation as an effective remedy for paired-data scarcity and imbalance across languages.
papers.venue: Accepted at NCMMSC 2026, to appear in Springer CCIS
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech llm

papers.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
papers.abstract: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech language model

# GRVL — Raspy Rock-Soul Power Vocals for YuE2

LoRAs that push [YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) toward a **raspy, gravelly, powerhouse female voice**: cool half-spoken verses that climb into belted, growling choruses and screamed high notes. The styles around the voice run from 1960s raw rhythm and blues, through 1980s arena pop-rock and soul-rock, to 1990s cinematic soul with strings and brass. English lyrics, female lead.

Each file patches **both halves** of YuE2: the autoregressive planner (writes the score and the vocal lines) and the flow-matching decoder (the sound). Trigger word: **`grvl`**. All six were trained with the experimental YuE2 trainer in [Ostris AI Toolkit](https://github.com/ostris/ai-toolkit), in two generations: **v1**, trained on a broader dataset with several raspy voice types, and **v2**, trained on a larger, more focused dataset.

The LoRAs use Comfy's fused YuE2 key layout (`text_encoders.*` for the planner, `diffusion_model.*` for the decoder). They load through the **[FS_Audio Suite](https://github.com/KytraScript/ComfyUI-FS_Audio_Suite)** LoRA loader and through Comfy's standard LoRA loader.

## Prompting

### Style prompt

Start with the trigger, then one descriptive sentence in the order the training captions used: language, era and genre, the voice, its delivery, instruments, mood, production, BPM. The prompts in `prompts/` are good starting points:

- `cinematic_noir`: 1990s cinematic soul, smoky low verses, belted choruses, strings and brass stabs, suspenseful, 102 BPM.
- `soul_ballad`: 1980s soul-rock ballad, electric piano, warm bass, synth pads, saxophone, 96 BPM.
- `cool_longing`: 1980s soul-pop, cool restrained verses rising to a belted chorus, synth flute, mid-tempo, 99 BPM.
- `raw_60s_soul`: 1960s classic soul and R&B, gritty verses, raw shouted choruses, horns and piano, 127 BPM.
- `arena_rock`, `power_ballad`, `husky_synthpop`: the v1 test prompts (big gated drums, a piano power ballad, and a husky half-spoken new-wave voice).

### Steering the voice

The two generations were captioned with different vocal vocabularies, and each file responds best to its own. Both sets of words work on both, and mixing them is fine.

**v2 files (Thunder, Tempest): delivery.** The more focused v2 dataset was captioned with one fixed voice phrase, `raspy gravelly alto female vocal`, followed by how it is sung. Verses and choruses are described separately, so you can write the arc of the song:

| delivery (as written in the captions) |
|---|
| cool restrained half-spoken delivery |
| smoky sultry low-register singing |
| tender soft-sung delivery |
| gritty mid-range soul singing |
| fierce powerful belting with growls |
| soaring sustained high notes |
| raw shouting with screams |

Pattern: `raspy gravelly alto female vocal, smoky sultry low-register singing in the verses, fierce powerful belting with growls in the choruses`. One mode for the whole song: `gritty mid-range soul singing throughout`. Extras the captions used: `screamed high notes`, `spoken asides`, `backing vocals`. Era words at the start of the genre (`1960s`, `1980s`, `1990s`) move the arrangement and the recording sound.

**v1 files (Ember, Smoulder, Cinder, Wildfire): voice types.** The broader v1 dataset covers four raspy voice types, each captioned with one fixed description:

- **Gravelly alto:** `raspy gravelly alto female vocal, fierce and soulful, powerful belting delivery with growled accents`
- **Husky mezzo:** `husky raspy mezzo female vocal, dramatic and yearning, powerful belting delivery with soaring sustained high notes`
- **Gritty mezzo:** `gritty powerful mezzo female vocal, bold and soulful, powerful belting delivery with soaring sustained high notes`
- **Husky low alto:** `low husky gravelly alto female vocal, cool and sultry, restrained half-spoken delivery`

The gravelly alto has the most v1 data and is the most reliable.

### Lyrics

Plain words, verses that tell a story, a chorus that repeats, a bridge: about 200–290 words plans a four- to five-minute song. Use YuE2 section tags on their own lines: `[Verse 1]`, `[Pre-Chorus]`, `[Chorus]`, `[Bridge]`, `[Outro]`. A `[Pre-Chorus]` that climbs gives the voice somewhere to go before the belted chorus.

### Which knob does what

- **File** first: Thunder for the most consistent voice, Tempest for the most character, Wildfire for the biggest v1 sound, Ember or Smoulder for a lighter touch.
- **strength_model (decoder)** changes the sound; **strength_clip (planner)** changes the writing. If the high end starts to sound thin, lower `strength_model` to ~0.8.
- **Seeds** decide the form as much as the lyric; try a few.

## Training

Lossless recordings of raspy, powerhouse female rock-soul and pop-rock vocals from the 1960s to the 1990s, as whole songs or halves cut at a pause between sung phrases. Tracks with a guest or duet lead vocal were left out. Captions were written by audio LLMs in YuE2's native descriptive style (Qwen Omni for the v2 style text, Gemini for delivery tags and lyrics), then rewritten by rule so the voice description uses the fixed vocabularies above; tempos were checked by hand.

Both generations: AI Toolkit YuE2 trainer, rank 32, LR 5e-5 with the planner at 0.4× (`ar_lr_multiplier` 0.4), planner KL 0.2, transcribed ABC scores (`cot full`) with 50 % score dropout.

- **v1 (Ember, Smoulder, Cinder, Wildfire):** the broader dataset, 36 items across four voice types, 800 steps (22 passes per item).
- **v2 (Thunder, Tempest):** the more focused dataset, 51 items spanning four decades, trained to 1100 steps. Past ~20 passes per item (step 1000+) the voice turned thin and tinny, so the release stops at step 950 (19 passes).

## Known limitations

- English, female lead only.
- A score can run past the length cap and the song ends abruptly; raise `song_length_cap` or shorten the lyric.
- Later checkpoints thin out the high end (why v2 stops at step 950); lower `strength_model` if you hear it.
- The 1960s prompts bring vintage recording character with them (narrower, rougher sound) by design.

```
grvl_smoulder.safetensors  118 MB   v1, step 500, same layout
grvl_cinder.safetensors    118 MB   v1, step 600, same layout
grvl_wildfire.safetensors  118 MB   v1, step 800, same layout
```

# YuE2 Turbo Radio

**Measured real-time music generation with YuE2 3B, now including Apollo's RTX 4080 CUDA port.**
This repository now contains the **actual Q8_0 model, F16 VAE, tokenizer and config files**,
plus the optimized source/runtime release and listening gallery. It is **not a new fine-tune**.
It uses [m-a-p/YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) via
[audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF) and
[audio.cpp](https://github.com/JarodMica/audio.cpp). The exact benchmarked model files are hosted here, unchanged from the attributed upstream GGUF release.

Weights are the unchanged audio-cpp conversion of m-a-p/YuE2-3B—not an original fine-tune.

## Listen: Knight Shift Radio

### [Tune in to Knight Shift Radio →](https://knight-shift-radio.vercel.app/)

Original YuE2 music, with warm Kasey song introductions and separate Jessica tech/AI information segments.
The show's direction is developed arrangements, thoughtful genre transitions and positive lyrics about
kindness, hard work and shared progress. Speech uses ElevenLabs separately from YuE2 music.
The public site is linked here; stream availability and the live rundown can change.
No claim is made that the samples below are currently scheduled or on air.

## Latest measured results — Apollo RTX 4080, 2026-11-02

RTX 4080 16 GB; CUDA 13.0, SM 8.9; Q8_0 YuE2-3B + F16 VAE. GPU clocks and power limits unchanged.
One warmup discarded, then **three separate measured cold CLI processes** per full-song configuration.
Speed is audio seconds / elapsed seconds. Session and startup-inclusive numbers are deliberately separate.

| Workload | NAR steps | Audio | Median session speed | Median including CLI startup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| city_lights, cache-off baseline | 8 | 69.00 s | 3.173× | 3.030× |
| city_lights, accepted full-song runtime | 8 | 69.00 s | **3.168×** | **3.019×** |
| Same accepted runtime | 32 | 69.00 s | **2.754×** | **2.648×** |
| Four-minute song | 8 | 257.08 s | **3.322×** | **3.269×** |

In practical terms, the 4:17 song takes about **79 seconds including CLI startup**.
At 32 steps, city_lights takes about **26 seconds including startup** for 69 seconds of audio.
The cache-on/off difference is within noise; **no CUDA prefix-cache speedup is claimed**.
Long-song NAR takes 10.09–10.19 s versus about 3.8–4.0 s on the short song: no superlinear
penalty was observed at the measured window size. This is not a universal scaling law.

- [Short-song runs](apollo/receipts/city-lights-results.json) · [Long-song runs](apollo/receipts/long-song-results.json)

### Streaming: first audio in 8.56–9.43 seconds, 3/3 passed

The adapter-safe asynchronous NAR preload runtime produces first audio **including cold CLI startup** at
**8.555, 9.165 and 9.432 seconds**. Each run naturally completes **256.839 s** of stereo PCM in
21 contiguous chunks, with **zero late chunks and zero gaps**. Its PCM is byte-identical to the original
streaming predecessor for this exact request. This does not claim bit parity between CUDA and SYCL,
model-quality parity, or tested LoRA output parity (adapter sources fall back to the ordinary loader).

The original, pinned-upload, retained-mapping and earlier-score variants that missed the latency gate
remain in the receipts. They are not promoted or silently hidden.
[All three accepted runs](apollo/receipts/stream-preload-v3-results.json) ·
[Accepted streaming identity](apollo/receipts/accepted-stream-artifact.json).

### Thirty-minute playlist: passed

**1,800 seconds of real-paced PCM consumption**, 86,400,000 stereo frames, zero queue failures,
zero fallback items and zero inserted-silence frames; expected/actual PCM SHA256 match.
This is an isolated producer/consumer soak, **not** a network-stream or physical-audio-device test,
and does not establish listener delivery or perfect musical transitions.
[Playlist receipt](apollo/receipts/playlist-soak-final-results.json).

The arrangements request evolving sections, instrumental interplay and a natural ending.

## B70 results and research — history retained, latest recheck disclosed

The previously published November 1 B70 measurements remain available:
**3.091× session realtime** on city_lights at 8 steps, **2.414×** at 32 steps,
**2.141×** on Knight Won't Stop at 32 steps, first streaming audio **7.58–7.73 s**,
and a passing 30-minute isolated queue. [Previous card and linked receipts](history/README-before-apollo-20261102.md).

The **November 2 canonical B70 recheck failed the 3.0× gate**, median **2.818×**
(2.818, 2.141, 2.939×). All three songs naturally completed and exceeded 55 seconds.
This does not erase the earlier pass and is not an Apollo result.
[Latest B70 recheck receipt](apollo/receipts/b70-required-recheck-results.json).
No new B70 GPU execution was performed for this publication.

Recent research/audits cover native sampler behavior, seed contract, generation defaults,
Q8/F16 cache and PCM rail accounting, VAE tiling, decoder precision and official-decoder comparisons.
These are **scoped experimental or diagnostic findings**, not all production improvements or end-to-end speedups.
[Research index](research/README.md) · [Evidence reconciliation](research/EVIDENCE-REVIEW-20261101.md).
The historical October recipe, charts and earlier songs remain in this repository;
[read the prior card](history/README-before-apollo-20261102.md) for that material.

## What changed on Apollo

The CUDA port carries over growing AR buffers, cached NAR prefixes, bounded NAR windows
(1024 frames / 128 overlap), and deferred packed-weight uploads from the B70 work.
CUDA Flash Attention and CUDA graphs replace Intel-specific kernels. An independent, opt-in streaming
pipeline overlaps safe NAR weight loading with earlier work and preserves the tested predecessor PCM.
The measured full-song runtime stays frozen; streaming has its own binary and source identity.
The older engine ignores `yue2.packed_projections` and `yue2.kv_cache_alignment` request keys:
they are retained where present in raw historical receipts, but receive no performance credit.

## Reproduce / download

Start with [Apollo build and run instructions](apollo/BUILD-AND-RUN.md).
The pinned source base, patches, source archive SHA256, accepted executable SHA256s,
model hashes and protocol receipts are included. Linux x86-64 CUDA executables are provided
as **experimental, hardware/environment-specific artifacts**, not a portable installer.
Rebuilding is supported by the recorded source recipe, but byte-identical rebuilds are not claimed.
Download the model and runtime together from this repo; the model remains **CC BY-NC 4.0**. Nothing in this release changes your radio queue.

## Limitations, attribution and licenses

These are local measured results, not official benchmark/leaderboard scores or a world-record claim.
No official-model waveform/quality parity is established. Cross-hardware sampled trajectories can differ.
Signal checks are not listening approval: some takes have PCM rail samples and naturally quiet tails.
The queue test does not certify internet delivery, actual loudspeaker output, host cadence or genre transitions.

- YuE2 3B / VAE: Multimodal Art Projection (m-a-p), **CC BY-NC 4.0**; GGUF conversion by audio-cpp.
- audio.cpp: ShugoAI LLC, **Apache-2.0**. Its bundled third-party components retain their licenses;
  the source archive includes those notices. SYCL EXPM1/concat work derives from ggml/llama.cpp (**MIT**).
- Project engine patches and scripts: Apache-2.0; model card, charts and generated music: CC BY-NC 4.0.
- The previous card preserves the detailed contributor/tool credits and historical release narrative.
  [NOTICE](NOTICE) records the existing licensing credits. Not affiliated with or endorsed by m-a-p,
  ShugoAI, NVIDIA, Intel, or the ggml authors.

Assamese is cross-lingual for every built-in voice; see [limitations](#limitations). ## Quickstart Use **Linux, Python 3.10–3.12, and an NVIDIA GPU with a driver supporting CUDA 12.8**. Start with `max_seats=1`. The documented single-seat loading peak is approximately 9.2 GB plus CUDA context; a 12 GB or larger GPU provides more room. See [hardware and memory](#hardware-and-memory) before increasing concurrency. ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install "maya3[server] @ git+https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native" \ --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 ``` ### Generate speech ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) audio = tts.generate( "नमस्ते, आपका ऑर्डर कल पहुँच जाएगा।", lang="hi", voice="Ahana", normalize=True, ) sf.write("speech.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` `generate()` returns a mono NumPy waveform in `float32`. Model weights, the Mimi codec, and the ECAPA speaker encoder are downloaded on first use. For offline inference, cache all three first, then set `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. **Normalization differs by interface:** the HTTP and WebSocket servers enable it by default. The Python API requires `normalize=True`. It expands numbers, currency, dates, times, URLs, email addresses, and other written forms into spoken text. Check the output for unusual formats.
Stream audio as it is generated ### Stream speech ```python from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) try: with open("speech.pcm", "wb") as output: for chunk in tts.stream( "Your order has shipped and will arrive tomorrow.", lang="en", voice="Siddhant", normalize=True, ): output.write(chunk.astype(" ### Clone a voice across languages Use a clean, single-speaker reference clip and its exact transcript. Obtain the speaker's permission before cloning their voice. The reference language and the output language can differ. ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) tts.register_voice( "my_voice", ref_audio="reference.wav", # 3–10 seconds recommended ref_text="", lang="hi", # reference language ) audio = tts.generate( "வணக்கம், எப்படி இருக்கிறீர்கள்?", lang="ta", # output language voice="my_voice", normalize=True, ) sf.write("cloned_voice_tamil.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` The default cloning mode, `icl_spk`, combines the reference audio with an ECAPA speaker embedding. Clones approximate the reference voice; similarity and accent vary. A dedicated cloning benchmark is not included in this release's reported results.
Run a local HTTP and WebSocket server ### Serve over HTTP or WebSocket ```bash python -m maya3.server \ --ckpt maya-research/maya2-native \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --max-seats 1 ``` After `GET /health` reports ready, generate speech: ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"input":"Your order has shipped.","language":"en","voice":"Ahana","response_format":"wav"}' \ --output speech.wav ``` The server provides `POST /v1/audio/speech`, `WS /v1/tts/stream`, and voice registration endpoints. It has no built-in authentication; add authentication and access controls before exposing it beyond a trusted environment. See the [GitHub README](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native#serve-the-model) for clients and protocol details.

Three ASR judges measured intelligibility; a speaker-embedding classifier measured consistency among the 20 built-in voices. **These are Maya Research's release measurements.** ASR error rates and embedding similarity capture specific aspects of quality; they do not replace human listening or measure every aspect of naturalness. Serving measurements below describe the tested hardware and workload. ### Benchmark design The release benchmark, **bench6k**, contains **6,000 held-out texts: 500 per language across 31 content categories**, including conversation, names, numbers, dates, currency, addresses, URLs, code-mixed text, tongue twisters, and prompts of 1–50 words. The release documentation states that these evaluation texts were excluded from training. The benchmark produced **20.3 hours of speech** through the server, with normalization and engine guards enabled, sampled decoding, and one seed per row. Voices were distributed across languages and categories; long inputs used the serving stack's text chunking. Three ASR systems transcribed the generated speech: - **ASR-1:** Maya's in-house Indic ASR and primary judge. - **Qwen3-ASR:** a third ASR judge. - **ASR-2:** a second in-house Indic ASR, held out from training, reward generation, and checkpoint selection. **Character error rate (CER)** compares ASR transcripts with spoken-form references. Scorer v1 uses the benchmark's normalization and script harmonization. Scorer v2 additionally harmonizes Latin and native-script spellings in code-mixed spans. The two scorers evaluate the same generated audio; lower v2 scores reflect a scoring change. | Overall CER ↓ | ASR-1 | Qwen3-ASR | ASR-2, held out | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Scorer v1 | 3.49% | 3.40% | 2.86% | | Scorer v2, additional code-mix harmonization | 2.35% | 2.22% | 1.73% | ### Results by language CER below uses **scorer v1**. Architecture and audio generation ## Architecture Maya 2 Native generates discrete audio tokens autoregressively, then decodes them into speech with Mimi. | Component | Description | |---|---| | Text and audio backbone | Initialized from [Qwen3-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base); 28 layers, hidden size 2,048, 16 attention heads and 8 KV heads; extended vocabulary for language and audio tokens | | Depth decoder | Approximately 555M parameters; predicts codebooks 1–31 after the backbone predicts codebook 0 | | Audio codec | [Kyutai Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/mimi); 32 codebooks with 2,048 entries each, at 12.5 frames per second | | Speaker conditioning | 192-dimensional [SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN](https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb) embedding projected into the backbone; reference-audio conditioning for cloning | | Output | 24 kHz mono speech, 80 ms per audio frame | At each step, the backbone predicts the first codebook, the depth decoder fills the remaining codebooks, and Mimi decodes an audio frame. The engine can emit that frame while generation continues. An end-of-audio token controls normal stopping; duration and loop guards provide additional controls.
## Training data and procedure The release documentation describes a mixture of **licensed and synthetic speech with transcripts** across the 12 languages, plus text-only data used to adapt the backbone to the languages. The built-in voice personas use synthetic and licensed voice data prepared for this purpose. The preference-optimization stage used **direct preference optimization (DPO)** on model-generated candidates ranked by ASR agreement and speaker similarity. Benchmark texts were excluded from training, according to the release documentation. Dataset identities, total training hours, detailed per-language composition, and the full training configuration are not disclosed in this release. Automated scores should be considered alongside these disclosure limits. ## Limitations - **Uneven language coverage.** Assamese is the most challenging Indic language in the release benchmark. No built-in voice has at least one hour of Assamese training data; some outputs drift toward a Bengali-like timbre. Other cross-lingual combinations can also carry the voice's training-language accent. - **Very short turns.** One- or two-word prompts are less stable in voice identity, and speaker-embedding evaluation is less reliable on very short clips. A slightly longer phrase may help short agent responses. - **Code-mixed and written-form inputs.** English words inside Indic sentences vary by voice. URLs, symbols, dates, and long digit sequences remain difficult, even with normalization. Listen to application-specific examples before relying on them. - **Voice cloning.** Similarity is approximate. Noise, multiple speakers, short references, and inaccurate transcripts can degrade results. Dedicated zero-shot cloning scores are not reported here. - **Emotion and events.** Tags such as `[laughs]`, `[sighs]`, `[whispers]`, `[sad]`, and `[excited]` are best effort and were not the focus of this release. - **Generation and guards.** Sampling can produce errors. The same seed is reproducible for an isolated request, but batching changes the random stream. Loop and duration guards can end genuinely repetitive text early. No benchmark clip spoke a built-in voice name aloud, but this remains a possible failure mode. - **Evaluation scope.** Results use automated ASR and speaker-embedding judges. This card does not report a human naturalness study, comprehensive dialect or demographic evaluation, confidence intervals, or a controlled comparison with other TTS models. ## Intended use and responsible deployment Maya 2 Native is intended for voice interfaces and agents, accessibility, reading and narration, IVR, notifications, and research on multilingual speech generation. Clone only voices you own or have explicit permission to use. Disclose synthetic speech to listeners, especially in calls and media. Do not use the model for deceptive impersonation, fraud, harassment, non-consensual content, disinformation, or attempts to defeat voice authentication. Built-in voice names identify synthetic personas and should not be presented as real people. **This release does not add an audio watermark.** Applications should implement the consent, disclosure, access controls, and abuse monitoring appropriate to their use. Consult the repository's [security guidance](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for deployment considerations.

[![GitHub](./assets/badges/github-badge.svg)](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS) [![License](./assets/badges/license-badge.svg)](./LICENSE) [![Demo](./assets/badges/demo-badge.svg)](https://edge0-ai.github.io/Audio8_TTS/realistic-0.6b/) [![arXiv](./assets/badges/arxiv-badge.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14776) [![Playground](./assets/badges/playground-badge.svg)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air) [Languages](#supported-languages) · [Quick start](#installation) · [Serving](#high-throughput-serving-sglang-omni) · [Evaluation](#evaluation)
--- **Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air** builds on [Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b), delivering **substantially improved speech realism** while retaining its compact **0.6B** architecture and zero-shot voice cloning capabilities. This release supports **23 languages**, adding **12 languages compared with Preview**. It uses the same Transformers inference interface as Preview. This repository includes the complete model checkpoint, its 44.1 kHz neural audio codec, tokenizer, processor, and custom Transformers code. Try speech generation and voice cloning in the [interactive Playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air). Hosted on Hugging Face ZeroGPU; availability depends on the queue and your daily GPU allowance. ## Highlights - **Improved realism:** more natural prosody and expressive delivery, building on Preview. - **Broader multilingual coverage:** 23 languages, including 12 additions to Preview's 11 supported languages. - **Compact model:** 601 million main-model parameters, with the audio codec bundled separately. - **Flexible generation:** zero-shot voice cloning from a reference recording and transcript, or speech generation without a reference. - **GPU serving:** an SGLang Omni adapter with paged attention, dynamic batching, and an OpenAI-compatible speech API. ## Supported Languages | Coverage | Languages | |---|---| | Supported in Preview (11) | Cantonese, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Spanish | | Added in Realistic Air (12) | Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese | > **Note:** Language quality varies; see the per-language evaluation below. Benchmark coverage includes some additional languages and is distinct from the supported-language list. ## Model Details Audio8 TTS uses a DualAR architecture inspired by [Fish Audio S2 Pro](https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech). The slow AR transformer predicts one semantic token for each audio frame. The fast AR transformer predicts the frame's codec codebooks, conditioned on the slow hidden state and preceding codebooks. | Component | Configuration | |---|---| | Main model | 601,159,424 parameters, excluding the codec | | Slow AR | 24 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads | | Fast AR | 4 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads | | Acoustic tokens | 10 codebooks, 4,096 entries per codebook | | Codec | 44.1 kHz, 2,048 samples per model frame (~21.5 frames/s) | | Context | Up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions | The bundled codec handles both reference-audio encoding and waveform decoding, so no additional codec checkpoint is required. The **0.6B** size refers to the main DualAR model; the codec is excluded from that parameter count. --- ## Installation Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable GPU are recommended. ```bash pip install "torch>=2.5.0" "torchaudio>=2.5.0" \ "transformers>=4.57.0,<5" "soundfile>=0.12" "safetensors>=0.4" ``` The Transformers release package was smoke-tested with PyTorch 2.8.0 and Transformers 4.57.3 on an NVIDIA H20 using BF16. Checks covered model loading, English and Chinese generation with and without reference audio, and generation in Arabic, Cantonese, Portuguese, and Russian. These are runtime checks, separate from the benchmark results below. ## Usage The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the files in this repository, then load it with `trust_remote_code=True`. ### Zero-shot voice cloning Use a clean reference recording. Its transcript must match the spoken content exactly. ```python import soundfile as sf import torch from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor model_id = "Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype, ).eval().to(device) inputs = processor( text=["Welcome to Audio8 TTS. It is wonderful to hear from you."], reference_audio=["reference.wav"], reference_text=["The exact transcript of the reference recording."], return_tensors="pt", ) inputs = {name: value.to(device) for name, value in inputs.items()} with torch.inference_mode(): output = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, top_k=50, do_sample=True, return_dict_in_generate=True, ) waveforms, waveform_lengths = model.decode_audio(output.codes) audio = waveforms[0, : int(waveform_lengths[0])].float().cpu().numpy() sf.write("output.wav", audio, model.config.codec_sample_rate) ``` ### Generation without a reference Replace the processor call above with: ```python inputs = processor( text=["This utterance does not use a reference voice."], return_tensors="pt", ) ``` Then move the inputs to the model device and run the same generation and decoding steps. For command-line inference, batching, and supervised fine-tuning, see the [Audio8 TTS repository](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS), using `Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air` as the model path. ## High-throughput serving: SGLang Omni The [SGLang Omni adapter](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS/tree/master/sglang_omni) provides GPU serving for Audio8 TTS. It is installed as an independent model plugin and does not overwrite SGLang Omni core files. | Capability | Support | |---|---| | Attention and batching | SGLang paged attention and dynamic batching | | DualAR execution | Slow AR serving with a fixed KV cache for the Fast AR codebook decoder | | Voice cloning | Reference-audio encoding and waveform decoding | | API | OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` service | Use the **0.6B** configuration, `sglang_omni/configs/audio8_tts_0_6b.yaml`, and set the model path to `Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air` or its downloaded snapshot. The adapter supports generation without a reference and zero-shot voice cloning. See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS#sglang-omni-serving) for compatible dependency versions, installation, server configuration, and API examples. > **Validation note:** Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air was tested on an NVIDIA H20 in BF16 for generation with and without a reference through the non-streaming speech API, with Torch compilation and CUDA graphs disabled. These checks validate runtime compatibility; throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. --- ## Evaluation Error rates are percentages (**lower is better**). Speaker similarity (SIM) is on a **0–1 scale** (**higher is better**). These metrics measure intelligibility and speaker similarity; they do not directly measure perceived speech realism. ### Benchmark summary **Audio8-TTS-Preview** and **Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air**, both **0.6B**: | Benchmark | Coverage | Preview error % ↓ | Realistic Air error % ↓ | Preview SIM ↑ | Realistic Air SIM ↑ | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Seed-TTS | English / Chinese | 1.23 | 1.25 | 0.682 | 0.704 | | CV3 | 8 shared languages | 4.80 | 4.56 | — | 0.663 | | CV3 | 9 core languages | — | 4.86 | — | 0.661 | | MiniMax | 24 evaluated languages | — | 5.89 | — | 0.754 | > **Note:** Values are unweighted language macro averages. Preview results are calculated from its [published model card](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b#evaluation), with SIM converted from percentages to a 0–1 scale. The two releases were evaluated separately. A dash means the corresponding result was not reported on Preview's card. > > Seed-TTS averages English WER and Chinese CER, excluding hard Chinese. The shared CV3 subset is Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish, and Italian; the 9-language set also includes Russian. CV3 averages exclude hard subsets and the 13 additional languages. MiniMax averages all 24 evaluated languages, including languages outside the supported list. ### Reference comparison The following error rates come from the sources used in our technical report. Different evaluation pipelines and text normalization make this a reference comparison rather than a strictly matched ranking. A dash means that a result is unavailable in the comparison, not that the model lacks support. | Model | Parameters (B) | Seed-TTS EN/ZH error ↓ | CV3 (9) error ↓ | MiniMax (24) error ↓ | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | **Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air** | **0.6** | **1.25** | **4.86** | **5.89** | | Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B | 0.6 | 1.12 | — | — | | Qwen3-TTS-1.7B | 1.7 | 1.01 | 7.73 | 27.41 | | Higgs Audio v3 | 4 | 1.11 | 4.41 | 2.74 | | Higgs Audio v2 | 4.7 | 1.17 | 4.49 | — | | Fish S2 Pro | 4.6 | 1.32 | 4.49 | 4.40 | | MOSS-TTS-v1.5 | 8.5 | 1.52 | 6.11 | 3.78 | | CosyVoice3-1.5B | 1.5 | 1.67 | 6.89 | — | | VoxCPM2 | 2.3 | 1.41 | 5.35 | — | > **Sources:** Qwen Seed-TTS results are from the Qwen3-TTS report, linked from the [official Qwen3-TTS repository](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-TTS); Qwen's CV3/MiniMax results, all Higgs Audio v3 results, and MOSS-TTS-v1.5's CV3/MiniMax results are from [Boson AI's evaluation](https://huggingface.co/bosonai/higgs-audio-v3-tts-4b). MOSS-TTS-v1.5's Seed-TTS result and the CosyVoice3/VoxCPM2 results are compiled in the [VoxCPM repository](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM). Cross-project SIM values are omitted because speaker encoders and evaluation conventions differ. > **Parameter conventions:** Audio8's 0.6B excludes its separate codec; Qwen and CosyVoice use release labels; Higgs Audio v3 uses its nominal **4B** release label. The remaining sizes are rounded checkpoint counts used in our report (VoxCPM2 excludes its separate AudioVAE). These counts use different conventions across systems. ### Seed-TTS detail | Split | Metric | Preview error % ↓ | Realistic Air error % ↓ | Preview SIM ↑ | Realistic Air SIM ↑ | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | English | WER | 1.506 | 1.464 | 0.632 | 0.663 | | Chinese | CER | 0.950 | 1.029 | 0.731 | 0.745 | | Chinese, hard | CER | 11.510 | 12.797 | 0.687 | 0.702 | > **Note:** Preview values are from its [published Seed-TTS table](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b#seed-tts), with SIM converted to a 0–1 scale. ### Multilingual detail

These hard subsets are excluded from the 9-language summary. Each of the 22 regular language rows contains 500 evaluation items. MiniMax: all 24 evaluated languages | Language | Metric | Error % ↓ | SIM ↑ | |---|---|---:|---:| | Arabic | CER | 2.403 | 0.7040 | | Cantonese | CER | 31.349 | 0.7710 | | Chinese | CER | 1.112 | 0.7950 | | Czech † | WER | 8.628 | 0.7330 | | Dutch | WER | 1.715 | 0.7050 | | English | WER | 2.161 | 0.7740 | | Finnish | WER | 5.072 | 0.7910 | | French | WER | 3.198 | 0.6660 | | German | WER | 0.898 | 0.7510 | | Greek † | CER | 4.181 | 0.7910 | | Hindi | CER | 9.209 | 0.8170 | | Indonesian | WER | 2.128 | 0.7270 | | Italian | WER | 1.958 | 0.7370 | | Japanese | CER | 5.142 | 0.7890 | | Korean | CER | 3.731 | 0.7850 | | Polish | WER | 1.957 | 0.7890 | | Portuguese | WER | 2.234 | 0.7860 | | Romanian † | WER | 17.425 | 0.7330 | | Russian | WER | 3.071 | 0.7490 | | Spanish | WER | 1.350 | 0.7450 | | Thai | CER | 6.674 | 0.7760 | | Turkish | WER | 1.560 | 0.7650 | | Ukrainian † | WER | 16.343 | 0.6940 | | Vietnamese | CER | 7.966 | 0.7120 | Each language has 100 evaluation items. # DuplexJev-32B-Para (v1.5)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Release notes: [hearing the whole clip (v1.5)](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-11-full-length.md) · [Japanese as a third language](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-japanese.md) · [weak languages](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-weak-languages.md) · Research notes: [hearing stress](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-stress-understanding.md) · [keeping a speech-decision LLM able to talk](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-chat-replay.md)

**The DuplexJev model that hears the most beyond the words.** On top of everything
[DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn) and
[DuplexJev-32B-Stress](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Stress) do (spoken QA, gender, emotion,
turn-taking, stress and pauses), it also hears **laughter, breathing, coughs and sighs**, notices **how** someone is
talking (whispering, shouting, very fast or slow), and can tell, roughly as a person would, **whether two clips are
the same speaker**. Mandarin and English. Since v1.1 it also **holds a normal conversation**, multi-turn included.
**v1.2** adds **accent judgments** (English accents and Mandarin dialect regions) and much sharper **end-of-turn
detection right after the user pauses**: on LiveKit's eot-bench it now beats Smart Turn v3.2 in English and Chinese.
**v1.3** hears **stress** much better: on the public StressTest benchmark it goes from 72 to **85**, on StressPresso's
meaning questions from 69 to **89**, and on choosing the meaning a stressed word implies (DEBATE, held-out) from 85 to **93**, with the
other decisions about the same.
**v1.4** understands far more languages: **Japanese** error goes from 33 % to **12 %** (FLEURS) and from 38 % to
**11 %** on conversational Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese error falls to a quarter to a third of v1.3, Thai,
Arabic and Russian error by 30–40 %, and Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (laughter, breath, drawl, stutter …) are much sharper.
**v1.5** hears the **whole clip**: earlier versions (like every Qwen3-ASR-based checkpoint we trained) dropped the
last ~4 % of every 30 s audio chunk, because the connector assumed 6.25 audio tokens per second while the encoder
emits 6.5. v1.5 is retrained on the true length, which sharpens the decisions that depend on the end of an utterance:
**end-of-turn** (Smart Turn test set 93.3 → **94.4**, Chinese 91.4 → **94.6**; LiveKit eot-bench English false
cut-offs at 300 ms 20.4 → **17.7 %**), **stress** (StressTest 81.7 → **85.3**), and **emotion** in natural speech
(LISTEN emotion 32.4 → **33.2**, LISTEN non-verbal 48.8 → **51.6**), with spoken QA up a point as well.

> **v1.5 (2026-11-03)** replaces v1.4 (2026-10-22): audio is read at its true length (`"audio_full_length": true`
> in `config.json`). **Use `duplexjev-vllm>=0.4` / `duplexjev>=0.7`**, which read this flag; older versions still
> load the model but cut the last ~4 % of each 30 s chunk, as before.
> Earlier versions stay available as revisions `v1.4`, `v1.3`, `v1.2`, `v1.1` and `v1.0` (`--revision v1.4` in vLLM,
> `revision="v1.4"` in `from_pretrained`).

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech as a **single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode
steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This repository is the complete model (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder
+ connector + the language model of Qwen3-VL-32B, 33.0 B parameters, bf16; one 80 GB GPU).

**Which 32B to pick.** This one, for everything above.

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-32B-Turn we trained the connector and a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here) for 4,000
steps. The mix is the 32B-Turn mix plus:

| added data | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| stress / pause detection (as in 32B-Stress: DEBATE, Stress-17K, TinyStress-15K, Expresso, neutral negatives) | which word is stressed, or none; where the pause is |
| speaker pairs (VoxCeleb1 dev, AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech, two-speaker mixtures) | same speaker or not; is this person in the clip |
| non-verbal sounds (VocalSound, NonVerbalSpeech-38K, NonverbalTTS, Expresso laughing) | is there laughter / breathing / a cough / a sigh / sniffing / throat clearing / a sneeze / crying …; negatives are cut from the same recordings away from the event |
| speaking style (EARS, Expresso whisper) | whispering, loud, fast, slow, high or low pitch, normal |
| spoken multiple-choice replay (ARC, OpenBookQA and CommonsenseQA train splits read by TTS) | keeps "answer the content" from being crowded out by "listen to the voice" |
| **v1.1:** conversation replay (spoken and typed user turns, up to 6 earlier turns as history; target = the original LLM's own reply) and in-house chat items | normal, full-length replies; trained with per-row loss averaging so long replies do not swamp the one-token decisions |
| **v1.2:** accents (VCTK, English Dialects, EdAcc, Common Voice accent labels, KeSpeech; held-out speakers kept for testing) | which accent: 19 English accents and 9 Mandarin dialect regions; native speaker or not; standard Mandarin or not; which English region |
| **v1.2:** end of turn right after a pause (otoSpeech-141h cut 0.2 s into each pause, with DualTurn labels; Smart Turn v3.2 training set) | finished vs. still talking / hesitating when the user has just gone quiet, the way a live voice agent has to decide |
| **v1.3:** the stress data re-balanced (more "which meaning does this stress imply" items, weight raised) and the gender data weighted ×2; no new corpora | choosing the meaning a stressed word implies; keeping gender where it was |
| **v1.4:** weak-language speech (ja, ko, vi, th, ar, ru: Emilia, Emilia-YODAS, YODAS2, Zeroth-Korean, VIVOS, FLEURS train, Common Voice; 162 k, labels re-checked with Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) + continuation (36 k) | transcribe and understand these languages |
| **v1.4:** Japanese speech (Emilia JA, Emilia-YODAS JA, Common Voice ja and other Japanese speech data; 358 k, re-checked) + Japanese continuation (20 k) | Japanese close to Chinese and English |
| **v1.4:** Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (licensed MagicData corpus, training speakers only; 42 k questions) | laughter, laughing while talking, breath, lip smack, sniff, cough, stressed word, drawl, which character is drawn out, stutter, sudden noise, unnatural pause, sentence emotion |
| **v1.4:** more emotion classes (surprise, fear, anxiety, excitement, encouragement, apologetic, playful) from CSEMOTIONS, EmotionTalk, DailyTalk, JL-Corpus, EMNS, Emozionalmente, SUBESCO | emotions beyond the basic four |

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" "duplexjev-vllm>=0.4"
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para --max-model-len 4096
```

`duplexjev-vllm>=0.4` reads `"audio_full_length": true` from `config.json` and feeds the whole clip; `DJ_FULL_LEN=0`
forces the old truncated length, `DJ_FULL_LEN=1` the full length for any checkpoint.

Prompt format and client are the same as for [DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn);
see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Examples:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Is there laughter in this audio?

Options:
A. Yes
B. No

Answer with the letter only.
```

```
用户说：<|audio|>

除了说话，这段音频里还有哪种声音？

选项：
A. 叹气
B. 咳嗽
C. 笑声
D. 都没有

请只回答选项字母。
```

Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions; the model was trained with it.

## Limitations

- Accent and same-speaker scores were not re-measured for v1.4 / v1.5.
- Thai and Arabic are still 2–3× the encoder's own error.
- Non-verbal training audio is mostly acted (radio drama, animation, studio recordings); in natural conversation the

- Speaker judgments are coarse (EER 18–40%) and must not be used to identify or verify people.

# OmniVoice Abkhazian (Finetuned)

This is a fine-tuned version of [k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://huggingface.co/spaces/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) for the **Abkhazian language** (`ab`). It was trained on a small, open dataset of Abkhazian speech to improve synthesis quality and prosody for this low-resource language.

## Model Details

- **Base model:** [k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://huggingface.co/spaces/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) — a diffusion-based TTS model supporting 600+ languages and zero-shot voice cloning.
- **Training data:** [Nart/abkhaz-tts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Nart/abkhaz-tts) (~10 hours of transcribed Abkhazian speech).
- **Language:** Abkhazian (`ab`).
- **Model size:** ~2.4 GB (fp16).
- **License:** Apache 2.0 (inherited from the base model).

## Intended Use

This model is intended for **research and non-commercial use**, specifically for:

- Generating Abkhazian speech from text.
- Voice cloning using a short reference audio (3–10 seconds) to control speaker identity and, importantly, **stress placement**.
- Building tools for language preservation and documentation.

## How to Use

### Installation

```bash
pip install omnivoice torch torchaudio
```

### Basic Inference (Voice Cloning with Reference)

The key feature for Abkhazian is using a **reference audio** to guide the model's prosody, especially stress. Provide a short clip of a native speaker (or yourself) pronouncing the target phrase or a similar phrase.

```python
import torch
import torchaudio
from omnivoice import OmniVoice

# 1. Load the fine-tuned model
model = OmniVoice.from_pretrained(
    "Grundik/omnivoice-abkhazian-finetuned",
    device_map="cuda:0",       # or "cpu" if you do not have a GPU
    dtype=torch.float16,
    load_asr=True,             # needed if you omit ref_text; model will auto-transcribe
)

# 2. Provide a reference audio (optional but recommended for stress control)
#    Replace "path/to/your/reference.wav" with the actual path to your file.
#    The audio should be clear speech, ideally 3-10 seconds.
ref_audio_path = "path/to/your/reference.wav"   # <-- CHANGE THIS

# 3. Generate speech
text_to_speak = "Анцәа длыцхраар, аиспан ԥҳәызба қәԥш валуаа ргерб даӷраԥало илкәаҳашт."

audio = model.generate(
    text=text_to_speak,
    language="ab",              # Abkhazian
    ref_audio=ref_audio_path,   # optional: guides stress and speaker identity
    # ref_text="...",          # optional: provide if you have transcription; otherwise ASR auto-transcribes
)

# 4. Save
torchaudio.save("output.wav", audio[0].cpu(), 24000)
print("Saved to output.wav")
```

### Without a Reference (Auto Voice)

If you do not provide a reference, the model will use a default voice. Quality and stress may vary.

```python
audio = model.generate(
    text="Анцәа длыцхраар, ...",
    language="ab",
)
```

## Limitations

- **Stress (ударение):** Abkhazian stress is complex and not fully predictable from text alone. The fine-tuned model has improved but not eliminated stress errors. Using a **reference audio** with correct stress is the recommended workaround.
- **Data size:** The training set (~10 hours) is small for TTS. The model may produce unstable results on out-of-domain text or long utterances.
- **Language coverage:** This checkpoint is specialized for Abkhazian; using it with other languages may yield unpredictable results.

## Training

- **Hardware:** Trained on a single consumer GPU (16 GB VRAM).
- **Data:** ~9.5 hours of Abkhazian speech with transcripts.
- **Fine-tuning type:** Full fine-tuning (not LoRA).

## Citation

If you use this model, please also cite the original OmniVoice paper:

```bibtex

  title={OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models},
```

# 🎙 Клонирование голоса в Colab — X-Voice + CosyVoice 3

Два готовых ноутбука Google Colab: клонирование **двух голосов**, кросс-язычная генерация (ru ⇄ en) и **диалог двух голосов** одним файлом.

| Ноутбук | Движок | Что делает |
|---|---|---|
| [`xvoice_colab.ipynb`](https://huggingface.co/Botoslav/voice-clone-colab/blob/main/xvoice_colab.ipynb) | **X-Voice Stage 2** (0.4B) | основной: клон голоса **без транскрипта**, 30 языков, диалог |
| [`cosyvoice3_colab.ipynb`](https://huggingface.co/Botoslav/voice-clone-colab/blob/main/cosyvoice3_colab.ipynb) | **CosyVoice 3** (0.5B) + Whisper | сравнение: авто-транскрипт референсов, Apache-2.0 (коммерция) |

## Запуск (3 шага)
1. Откройте ноутбук из таблицы выше → справа вверху кнопка **Open in Colab**.
2. В Colab: `Среда выполнения → Сменить среду выполнения → T4 GPU`.
3. `Среда выполнения → Выполнить всё`; в ячейке загрузки выберите два аудио-референса (5–27 сек чистой речи каждый).

Результаты появятся плеерами прямо в ноутбуке + архивом в конце.

## Нужен ли HF-токен?
Нет — X-Voice, Vocos и CosyVoice 3 публичные, скачивание работает и так. С токеном стабильнее (без рейт-лимитов): в Colab откройте панель **Секреты** (🔑 слева) → «Добавить секрет» → имя `HF_TOKEN`, значение — ваш токен с https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens. Ноутбуки подхватят его автоматически.

## Что внутри
- **X-Voice** — Stage 2: референс без транскрипта → речь на любом из 30 языков; лицензия весов CC-BY-NC-4.0 (некоммерческое).
- **CosyVoice 3** (Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512) — zero-shot с транскриптом (достаётся Whisper'ом автоматически); Apache-2.0.
- Диалоговый режим: реплики двух голосов чередуются и склеиваются в один WAV (24 кГц).

## Ресурсы

# Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b — LiteRT

This repository is a conversion to LiteRT of [`Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air) (renamed from `Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b`), made with litert-torch 0.9.4 and ai-edge-quantizer 0.9.0 for LiteRT 2.2.0: in the Android app under [`android/`](https://huggingface.co/litert-community/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b/tree/main/android), a Pixel 11 Pro speaks an 18-token English sentence (5.48 s of audio) at a real-time factor of 0.853, and a Galaxy S26 at 0.797 (6.36 s of audio), each the median of 6 runs (2026-11-03). The real-time factor is the time from text to samples divided by the length of the speech: below 1, the speech is ready before it would have finished playing.

[`Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air`](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air) is a text-to-speech model by Edge0, built on Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b. Its model card says that it supports 23 languages, and that it clones a voice zero-shot from a reference recording and its transcript or speaks without a reference. It uses a DualAR design inspired by Fish Audio S2 Pro: a 24-layer slow transformer predicts one semantic token per audio frame (2,048 samples, 46 ms at 44.1 kHz), a 4-layer fast transformer predicts the frame's 10 codec codebooks one at a time, and a neural codec turns the frames into audio. The transcript must match the reference recording exactly. A cloned voice speaking another language than its recording's: see Limitations.

This repository holds five LiteRT graphs (slow AR, fast AR, the codec decoder in two window sizes, the codec encoder), the source repository's tokenizer, two reference voices, a Python host loop for desktops and an Android sample app. The two autoregressive graphs hold int8 weights with float activations (dynamic-range quantization) and run on the CPU. In the app the codec decoder runs on the GPU; if the GPU's output fails a check at load, the same file runs on the CPU.

## Quick start (Python, desktop)

```bash
pip install ai-edge-litert tokenizers soundfile scipy numpy huggingface_hub
hf download litert-community/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b --local-dir audio8r
cd audio8r
python audio8_tts_litert.py --model-dir . --text "Hello from LiteRT, fully on device." \
    --voice voices/en_librispeech_1272 --out hello.wav
# Japanese with the bundled Japanese voice
python audio8_tts_litert.py --model-dir . --text "今日は天気が良いので、公園まで散歩に行きましょう。" \
    --voice voices/ja_funasr_example --out konnichiwa.wav
# clone your own voice from a clip of up to 10 s and its exact transcript
python audio8_tts_litert.py --model-dir . --register-voice me.wav --ref-text "exact transcript of me.wav" --voice-out voices/me
python audio8_tts_litert.py --model-dir . --text "This sentence is spoken in my voice." --voice voices/me --out me_out.wav
# without a reference voice
python audio8_tts_litert.py --model-dir . --text "This utterance does not use a reference voice." --out noref.wav
```

The host loop runs every graph on the CPU through the ai-edge-litert Interpreter (`--threads`, default 4). It uses the sampler of the source repository's `generation_config.json` (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9, top-k 50, at most 512 frames) and the vendor's repetition-aware re-draw; `--temperature`, `--top-p`, `--top-k`, `--max-new-tokens` and `--seed` change them. The source model card's own example samples at temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, top-k 50. The host loop prefills a prompt in chunks through the smallest prefill signature that holds what is left of it (`prefill_64` or `prefill_256`). XNNPACK packs the slow graph's weights separately for each of its three signatures, so the third one costs memory: on an Apple M4 Max with ai-edge-litert 2.2.0, generating the frames of four test sentences peaked at 2,074.7 MiB of resident memory, against 1,670.6 MiB with this repository's first slow file, which had no `prefill_64` (2026-11-03). The Android app keeps one packed copy in a weight cache file (below).

## Android

The app under [`android/`](https://huggingface.co/litert-community/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b/tree/main/android) (Kotlin, LiteRT 2.2.0 CompiledModel API) speaks a typed sentence in one of the two bundled voices, or in your own voice: "Record my voice (10 s)" records you reading a sentence it shows, and that sentence becomes the voice's transcript. Both AR graphs run on the CPU with 4 threads; the slow AR updates its KV cache in place and prefills a prompt in chunks of 256 positions, a last chunk of up to 64 positions through `prefill_64`. At load the app creates and warms both GPU codec decoders, runs the 128-frame one on one test window and compares its output with the CPU output of the same file on the same codes (that CPU output is bundled in the app); the GPU decodes when the correlation is 0.99 or more, the CPU otherwise. A sentence may have up to 49 tokens. Build, install and file push steps: [`android/README.md`](https://huggingface.co/litert-community/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b/blob/main/android/README.md). The app's code is under the MIT license (`android/LICENSE`).

Changes since this repository's first release (2026-11-02), measured in the app on both phones:

- **Weight cache.** Without a cache, XNNPACK packs the slow AR's weights again for each of the graph's three signatures at every load. The app writes the packed weights once to a file in the `xnnpack/` folder of its cache directory (named by the SHA-256 of `slow_ar_int8.tflite` and the LiteRT version; 365,205,496 bytes on the Pixel 11 Pro, 365,259,896 on the Galaxy S26) and maps that file at every later load. Peak resident memory of the app process after load (VmHWM): 2.01 GB on the Pixel 11 Pro and 2.31 GB on the Galaxy S26, against 3.13 and 3.39 GB with the first release's slow file without a cache (2026-11-03). Each load hashes the 558 MB slow file first: 0.3 to 1.0 s on the Pixel 11 Pro, 0.2 s on the Galaxy S26. The first load after installing also writes the cache and compiles the GPU's programs: 23.9 and 45.4 s in two first loads on the Pixel 11 Pro. Android may delete the cache folder when storage runs low, and the next load writes the file again; if the slow graph cannot be created with the cache, the app creates it without.
- **Prompt prefill.** With a bundled voice, the prompts of the two test sentences below (231 and 236 positions) are one 256-position chunk. A voice recorded in the app makes the prompt longer, and the part past 256 positions now runs as one `prefill_64` call instead of a padded `prefill_256` call. For an English sentence of 12 tokens (283 positions) and a Japanese one of 48 tokens (319 positions) in a recorded voice, the prompt prefill took 235 and 233 ms on the Galaxy S26 against 339 and 330 ms, and 514 and 745 ms on the Pixel 11 Pro against 972 and 1,163 ms (medians of 6 runs, 2026-11-03). In each Pixel 11 Pro process (12 sentences, in both forms), the slow AR slowed from about 12 to 16–27 ms per frame from the 4th, 5th or 6th sentence on, under CPU frequency caps.
- **Load.** The app creates and warms the 192-frame GPU decoder at load, and checks the GPU's output against the bundled CPU output instead of decoding the test window again on the phone's CPU. With the GPU's compiled programs on the phone, load took 8.71 s on the Pixel 11 Pro and 6.92 s on the Galaxy S26, against 19.21 and 10.86 s with the first release's load path (means of 2 app processes, 2026-11-02). On the Galaxy S26 the English test sentence (137 frames) no longer creates the 192-frame decoder in the first run of a process: its codec decode took 1.40 and 1.41 s there, against 2.38 and 2.30 s.
- **Frame cap.** When a sentence stops at the frame cap, the app's message gives the cap in frames and seconds as set (512 frames, 23.8 s, by default) and its log gets a `FRAME_CAP` line; the host loop prints a `[cap]` line.

## Codec decoder on the GPU

The two codec decoders as first published in the Preview repository gave a wrong output on the LiteRT GPU accelerator: on a Pixel 11 Pro and a Galaxy S26 (OpenCL, LiteRT 2.2.0 and 2.3.2) and on an Apple M4 Max (Metal), at the GPU's default precision (float16) and at float32. The Preview repository has carried the rewritten decoders since 2026-11-02 (commit `3d59a74c`). The decoders here carry three graph changes:

- Before two MUL operators whose non-constant operand (computed at run time) has rank 2 and the output rank 3, a RESHAPE gives the operand the output's shape. The GPU accelerator lays such a rank-2 tensor out differently from a rank-3 one, and the MUL then multiplied the wrong elements, at float32 too. The RESHAPE keeps the values and their order.
- Each RMSNorm squares its input scaled by 1/16, with epsilon scaled by 1/256 and the result scaled back. Unscaled, one square reaches 121,972.6 and the 1,024-channel sums of squares about 76,500, both more than float16 holds (65,504), and the output stops depending on the codes. Powers of two only move the exponent, so the CPU result is the same.
- The attention mask's −1e9 becomes −30000. In float16 −1e9 is −inf, and in the 192-frame decoder a row with no finite score turned into NaN.

On an Apple M4 Max CPU, the rewritten decoders give the original's output byte for byte on all 32 test code sequences (15 for 128 frames, 17 for 192). On the GPUs of both phones at the default precision, their output correlates with that CPU output at 0.9998 or more on every speech test sequence, and the Pixel 11 Pro run in Accuracy decodes on the GPU. The rewrite is `codec_gpu_rewrite.py` in [hf-to-litertlm](https://github.com/john-rocky/hf-to-litertlm) (`audio8_tts_work/`).

## Accuracy

The reference is the vendor's own code at revision `1e857568` in float32 on the CPU (PyTorch 2.12.1, transformers 4.57.6), with the sampler of `generation_config.json` and seeded draws. The test set has 30 sentences in six of the 23 languages: 6 English and 6 Japanese with a reference voice of the same language; 3 each in Arabic, Portuguese, Russian and Turkish without a reference, and 1 each of those four with the English reference voice; one English and one Japanese without a reference. Set B repeats set A with every sampling seed raised by 100,000. Each output was transcribed by whisper large-v3-turbo and compared with its text (errors counted in words, in characters for Japanese), compared with the reference clip by TitaNet-L (speaker cosine), and scored by UTMOS22.
